documents.title: Guidelines for the Use of Generative AI Tools
documents.summary: The provost's message tells the community to follow general guidelines on data privacy, verification, security and purchasing, and to follow instructor rules for coursework. It encourages experimenting with AI but leaves course permissions to instructors.
documents.stance_why: Stance is encourage because the letter says "We encourage you to experiment with AI tools" and ends "we will embrace technological tools"; the restrictions are about data and credentials, and coursework rules are only deferred to instructors, not set.

units.why: Statement of the provost's stance: "We encourage you to experiment with AI tools" welcomes AI use for the whole community, so it is a default-permit/encourage rule (P02), addressed to all, general, with a soft "encourage" modality (should).
units.anchor: We encourage you to experiment with AI tools.
units.frag_start: We encourage you to experiment

units.why: "align with existing university policies and uphold our institutional commitment to safety, security, and academic integrity" ties AI use to existing university rules, which is P77 (comply with existing policy); it is not P56 because it names no new framework principles.
units.anchor: which align with existing university policies
units.frag_start: please adhere to the following general guidelines
units.fit_note: The sentence also names safety and security commitments as the purpose of the guidelines.

units.why: "Do not enter confidential or legally restricted data" is a prohibition on what goes into AI tools, about data protection, so P50 (protect personal and confidential data), not P20 which concerns assignment specs and student code.

documents.title: Guiding Principles: Teaching and Learning with AI
documents.summary: Poorvu Center principles from 2026 on AI in teaching and learning: ownership, discussion with students, attention to disciplinary change, privacy and transparency. Instructors decide whether and how students use AI.
documents.stance_why: Stance is delegates because "instructors at Yale have full authority to determine whether and how students may use AI"; the document gives principles and says some courses may restrict while others may incorporate AI, with no default rule.

documents.title: Academic Dishonesty (Undergraduate Regulations)
documents.summary: The undergraduate academic integrity regulation contains one paragraph on AI: unattributed AI text is a violation, unauthorized AI use may be a breach, and permission varies by instructor. Students should check with the instructor.
documents.stance_why: Stance is delegates because the paragraph says whether instructors permit AI "will vary widely from course to course, and is always subject to each instructor’s authority and policy"; the only fixed rule is attribution.

units.why: "Inserting AI-generated text into an assignment without proper attribution is a violation of academic integrity" makes nondisclosure of AI text the violation itself, which is P28; P36 (misconduct) also applies but P28 is specific to attribution.
units.anchor: Inserting AI-generated text into an assignment without proper attribution is a violation of academic integrity
units.frag_start: Inserting AI-generated text into an assignment

notes: Coder B. Only the four included university-layer documents were coded; no school or computing documents were found and course syllabi are deferred. Non-AI parts of the academic-integrity regulation (multiple submission, exam cheating with devices, general plagiarism, labs) were not coded as they say nothing about AI. Navigation and archive lists in the Provost and Poorvu pages were skipped. The Clarity AI Platform and AI Literacy Framework appear only as link labels and were not coded as policies.
